summary: This Best Current Practice describes the structure, content, construction and meaning of language tags, such as those indicating the language of a document. It also covers registering values and private-use extensions. With RFC 4647 it replaced RFC 3066. It was later replaced by RFC 5646.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the short codes that say what language something is written in, such as en-US or zh-Hant. It fixes the order of the parts, says how each part is registered, and requires that the parts be recognisable from their shape alone so any program can read them.

subtitle: How to build and register the short hyphenated tags, like en-US or zh-Hant, that label which language content uses.

tldr.problem: Software needs a short, unambiguous way to say which language a document, a page or a request is in, so it can pick a translation, a spell checker, a speech synthesiser or a font.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is built from subtags separated by hyphens: a primary language subtag first, then optional script, region and variant subtags, then extensions and private use. Each subtag type is recognisable from its length and position alone, so a parser can read a tag without the registry.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4646 was a Best Current Practice and has been obsoleted by RFC 5646.

facts.label: Minimum tag length a protocol must allow

sections.title: What a Language Tag Is For
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a plain fact: human beings have used a number of languages, and there are many reasons to identify the language used when presenting or requesting information.

A user's language preferences often need to be identified so that appropriate processing can be applied. The user's language preferences in a web browser can be used to select web pages appropriately, and can also be used to select among tools such as dictionaries. Knowledge about the particular language used by some piece of information content might be useful or even required by some types of processing, for example spell-checking, computer-synthesized speech, Braille transcription, or high-quality print renderings.

One means of indicating the language used is to label the information content with an identifier, or tag. These tags can be used to specify user preferences when selecting information content, or for labeling additional attributes of content and associated resources. They can also indicate additional language attributes of content, for example the dialect, writing system or orthography used in a document.

The document specifies an identifier mechanism, the language tag, and a registration function for the values used to form tags. It also defines a mechanism for private use values and for future extension. In combination with RFC 4647 it replaces RFC 3066, which had replaced RFC 1766.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag tells a program what to do with a piece of content: which translation to offer, which dictionary to consult, which pronunciation rules to apply.

sections.title: The Syntax of a Language Tag
sections.content:
A language tag is composed of one or more parts, known as subtags. Each subtag consists of a sequence of alphanumeric characters, and subtags are separated from one another by a hyphen. A language tag consists of a primary language subtag and a possibly empty series of subsequent subtags, each of which refines or narrows the range of languages identified by the overall tag.

Usually, each type of subtag is distinguished by length, position in the tag and content, so subtags can be recognized solely by these features. The only exception is a fixed list of grandfathered tags registered under RFC 3066. This makes it possible to construct a parser that can extract and assign some semantic information to the subtags even if the specific subtag values are not recognized, so a parser need not have an up-to-date copy, or any copy at all, of the subtag registry to perform most searching and matching operations.

All subtags have a maximum length of eight characters, and whitespace is not permitted in a language tag. The tags and their subtags, including private use and extensions, are to be treated as case insensitive: there exist conventions for the capitalization of some subtags, but these must not be taken to carry meaning. ISO 639-1 recommends that language codes be written in lowercase, ISO 3166-1 recommends that country codes be capitalized, and ISO 15924 recommends that script codes use lowercase with the initial letter capitalized. The uppercase letters are considered equivalent to their lowercase equivalents, so the tag "mn-Cyrl-MN" is not distinct from "MN-cYRL-mn". Consistent formatting still helps users, and the recommended format is that all non-initial two-letter subtags are uppercase, all non-initial four-letter subtags are titlecase, and all other subtags are lowercase.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag is a few short words joined by hyphens, and each word's shape tells you what it is. Case never matters, though there is a preferred way to write them.

sections.title: The Subtag Types
sections.content:
The namespace of language tags and their subtags is administered by IANA, and the Language Subtag Registry maintained by IANA is the source for valid subtags. Each subtag type has unique length and content restrictions, so the type of a subtag can be determined without consulting the registry.

The primary language subtag is the first subtag in a tag and cannot be omitted. All two-character language subtags come from ISO 639 Part 1, and all three-character ones from ISO 639 Part 2. The range 'qaa' through 'qtz' is reserved for private use, all four-character language subtags are reserved for possible future standardization, and subtags of 5 to 8 characters are registered through the registration process and may be used as the primary language subtag. The single-character subtag 'x' as the primary subtag indicates that the tag consists solely of subtags whose meaning is defined by private agreement, so in the tag "x-fr-CH" the subtags 'fr' and 'CH' should not be taken to represent French or Switzerland unless a private agreement says so. The single-character subtag 'i' is used by some grandfathered tags such as "i-klingon".

The script subtag uses four-character ISO 15924 codes and must immediately follow the primary language subtag and any extended language subtags. At most one may appear, and it should be omitted when it adds no distinguishing value. "sr-Latn" represents Serbian written using the Latin script.

The region subtag is either a two-letter ISO 3166-1 country code or a three-digit UN M.49 code, must follow any language, extended language or script subtags, and at most one may appear. "de-CH" is German as used in Switzerland, and "es-419" is Spanish appropriate to the UN-defined Latin America and Caribbean region.

The variant subtag indicates additional well-recognized variations that are not covered by other subtags. It is not associated with any external standard and is defined by the registration process, must be registered before use, and must follow all the other defined subtags while preceding any extension or private use sequence. A variant starting with a letter must be at least five characters long and one starting with a digit at least four. "sl-nedis" represents the Natisone or Nadiza dialect of Slovenian, and "de-CH-1996" German as used in Switzerland with the spelling reform beginning in 1996.

Extension subtags are introduced by a single-character singleton other than 'x', and must follow at least a primary language subtag, so "a-value" is not a well-formed language tag while "de-a-value" is. Each singleton may appear at most once in a tag, and every subtag between one singleton and the next belongs to that extension, so in "fr-a-Latn" the subtag 'Latn' is not the script subtag. Private use subtags follow the reserved singleton 'x', must follow all other subtags, and have no source and no defined meaning outside a private agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: The parts come in a fixed order and each part is distinguishable by its length: a language, then optionally a writing system, then a country, then a registered variation, then any private additions.

sections.title: The IANA Language Subtag Registry
sections.content:
The Language Subtag Registry contains a comprehensive list of all the subtags valid in language tags. It is maintained so that, except for extension subtags, it is possible to validate all the subtags that appear in a language tag, and so that the meaning of the subtags is unambiguous and stable over time. The meaning of private use subtags is, of course, not defined by the registry.

The registry is a machine-readable text file in a record-jar format. Each line of text is limited to 72 characters including all whitespace, and records are separated by lines containing only the sequence "%%". Each field is a field-name and a field-body separated by a colon, and the field-body may be folded across lines. The sequence '..' in a field-body denotes a range of values, so 'a..c' denotes the values 'a', 'b' and 'c'. Characters outside the US-ASCII repertoire, and the ampersand, are represented by a numeric character reference in the style used by XML. The first record in the file contains the single field whose field-name is "File-Date", holding the last modification date of that copy.

Each record must contain a Type field, whose value is one of language, extlang, script, region, variant, grandfathered or redundant; either a Subtag field or a Tag field; a Description field; and an Added field holding the date the record was added. Records may also contain Preferred-Value, Deprecated, Prefix, Comments and Suppress-Script. The Preferred-Value field contains a mapping to a subtag or tag that is strongly recommended in place of the record's own value, and records with a Preferred-Value must also carry a Deprecated field with a date.

Maintenance is handled by the Language Subtag Reviewer, who is appointed by the IESG for an indefinite term, moderates the ietf-languages mailing list, responds to registration requests and performs the other registry maintenance duties. Only the Language Subtag Reviewer is permitted to ask IANA to change, update or add records.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps one authoritative list of every valid subtag. The list is plain text in a simple format, and one named reviewer is responsible for keeping it up to date.

sections.title: Choosing, Forming and Canonicalizing Tags
sections.content:
When several tags could describe the same text, interoperability is best served when all users use the same tag, so users are strongly recommended not to define their own rules. Subtags should only be used where they add useful distinguishing information. Use as precise a tag as possible, but no more specific than is justified: 'de' might suffice for an email written in German, while "de-CH-1996" is probably unnecessarily precise. The script subtag should not be used unless the script adds distinguishing information, so 'Latn' should not be used with 'en' because nearly all English documents are written in the Latin script. If a tag or subtag has a Preferred-Value, that value should be used, for example 'he' for Hebrew in preference to 'iw'. The 'und' subtag should not be used to label content even if the language is unknown, and 'mul' should not be used whenever the protocol allows separate tags for multiple languages.

What a tag means depends on where it appears. For a single information object the tags might be the set of languages needed for complete comprehension; for an aggregation they might be the languages used inside its components; for alternatives they might be a hint that the content is provided in several languages. In markup languages such as HTML and XML, language information can be added to each part of the document identified by the markup structure. Tags that share a prefix are related, so "zh-Hant-TW" is more specific than "zh-Hant", but that relationship is not guaranteed: languages that begin with the same sequence of subtags are not guaranteed to be mutually intelligible, since "az" shares a prefix with both "az-Latn" and "az-Cyrl".

On length, the syntax imposes no fixed upper limit on the number of subtags, but implementations should not truncate language tags unless the meaning is purposefully being changed or the tag does not fit a limited buffer size specified by a protocol, and they should warn the user when a tag is truncated. Protocols that specify limited buffer sizes for language tags must allow for language tags of up to 33 characters, and should allow for at least 42 characters.

Canonicalization gives one form of each tag. A tag is in canonical form when it is well-formed, when region subtags with a Preferred-Value have been replaced, when redundant or grandfathered tags with a Preferred-Value have been replaced, when other subtags with a Preferred-Value have been replaced, and when more than one extension sequence is ordered into case-insensitive ASCII order by singleton. Thus "en-A-aaa-B-ccc-bbb-x-xyz" is canonical while "en-B-ccc-bbb-A-aaa-X-xyz" is well-formed but not canonical. Case regularisation is optional, but implementers should specify a locale-neutral casing operation, because case folding of ASCII letters in certain locales, such as Turkish and Azerbaijani, produces a character value that is illegal in language tags.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the least specific tag that still says something useful, and write it in one standard order so that two programs comparing tags agree on whether they are the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Language tags used in content negotiation, like any other information exchanged on the Internet, might be a source of concern because they might be used to infer the nationality of the sender and thus identify potential targets for surveillance. This is a special case of the general problem that anything sent is visible to the receiving party and possibly to third parties as well. The evaluation of the exact magnitude of the threat, and any possible countermeasures, is left to each application protocol.

The RFC also makes two specific points. The language tag associated with a particular information item is of no consequence whatsoever in determining whether that content might contain possible homographs: the fact that a text is tagged as being in one language or using a particular script subtag provides no assurance whatsoever that it does not contain characters from scripts other than the one associated with the tag. And because there is no limit to the number of variant, private use and extension subtags, and consequently no limit on the possible length of a tag, implementations need to guard against buffer overflow attacks.

Finally, although the specification of valid subtags for an extension must be available over the Internet, implementations should not mechanically depend on it being always accessible, to prevent denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A language tag can hint at where a sender is, and it says nothing at all about whether the text really is in that language. Programs also have to cope with tags of any length.

viz.caption: THE SYNTAX OF A LANGUAGE TAG (RFC 4646)

data.title: The grammar of a language tag
data.code:
Language-Tag = langtag
             / privateuse
             / grandfathered

langtag     = (language
              ["-" script]
              ["-" region]
              *("-" variant)
              *("-" extension)
              ["-" privateuse])

language   = (2*3ALPHA [ extlang ])
           / 4ALPHA
           / 5*8ALPHA

script     = 4ALPHA
region     = 2ALPHA / 3DIGIT
variant    = 5*8alphanum / (DIGIT 3alphanum)
extension  = singleton 1*("-" (2*8alphanum))
privateuse = ("x"/"X") 1*("-" (1*8alphanum))

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF A LANGUAGE TAG

items.title: Primary language
items.text: The language itself, such as 'de' for German.

items.title: Script
items.text: The writing system, such as 'Hant' for traditional Chinese.

items.title: Region
items.text: A country or area, such as 'CH' for Switzerland or '419' for Latin America and the Caribbean.

items.title: Variant
items.text: A further registered variation, such as '1901' for a German spelling reform.

items.title: Extension
items.text: A single-letter prefix with subtags whose meaning the extension defines.

items.title: Private use
items.text: Subtags after 'x', meaningful only to the parties that agreed on them.
